episode_thesis: Systematic Investor Ep.377 (recorded early Dec 2025): trend following had a flat 2025 after policy shocks, but choppy regimes have always ended when fundamentals shifted, so investors should hold long-term. Alan Dunne argues the world has moved from 40 years of disinflation to a regime of stickier inflation, higher debt, rising global yields and a more positive stock-bond correlation, and that portfolios built on old labels (alternative/traditional) are over-concentrated in growth and stable inflation. His remedy is a risk-based 40% growth / 40% adaptive (trend, macro) / 20% diversifier portfolio built with futures leverage and return stacking, which beats 60/40 mainly through smaller drawdowns.

speakers.name: Alan Dunne
speakers.role: Archive Capital; co-host; author of the regime-adaptive portfolio paper
speakers.speaker_note: Transcript spells the name 'Alan Don'; the ledger identifies Alan Dunne. Speaker turns are unlabelled in the caption but the content (own paper, own portfolio) makes attribution clear.

worldview_premises.premise: Choppy, policy-shock periods for trend following end when fundamentals change and new information produces breakouts ('this too shall pass').
worldview_premises.support: Historical episodes: 2012 risk-on/risk-off ended with weak growth, breakouts in Bund, euro, oil; late-2010s slump eased from 2019; COVID ended secular stagnation.

worldview_premises.premise: Trends outlast consensus commentary: widely held bearish calls (e.g. Swiss franc/yen crosses) can be wrong for years while the trend persists.
worldview_premises.support: Anecdote: the Swiss franc/yen bearish call heard 'so many times in the last two years' while it kept rising.

worldview_premises.premise: The 1980-2020 regime was a 40-year disinflation / great moderation driven by Volcker, China's trade entry, Soviet collapse, free-market consensus and central bank independence; since 2020 inflation is higher, stickier and shock-prone and the bond-equity correlation is less stable and more positive.
worldview_premises.support: Historical narrative; change in bond market behaviour; no formal test given on the show.

worldview_premises.premise: Long-term yields are set by the savings-investment balance: excess savings and capital-light tech pushed them down (conundrum, negative yields), but AI/data-centre capex, defence spending and no appetite for austerity now push them up.
worldview_premises.support: Observed global yield rises (JGB, German 25-year) without news; US 10-year ~4.1% as the outlier.

worldview_premises.premise: The 1990s tech-boom parallel to AI is superficial: then, productivity came from diffusing PCs while internet capex added demand; now AI adds to GDP arithmetically through spending but productivity evidence is mixed, and debt/GDP is double with the 1999 surplus gone.
worldview_premises.support: McKinsey adoption study (more trying than using), St. Louis Fed study (marginal gains), debt/GDP comparison.

worldview_premises.premise: High debt combined with high equity valuations is a joint vulnerability: a recession steps debt/GDP up, households hold ~$40T equities so a bear market is a ~$20T wealth hit, raising the chance of fiscal dominance and financial repression.
worldview_premises.support: Debt/GDP step pattern in each recession; former IMF chief economist estimate; 'I don't hear a lot of people joining the dots'.

worldview_premises.premise: Tariffs hit unemployment immediately, lower inflation first, then raise inflation over the following two years, so markets pricing Fed cuts with inflation above target are complacent.
worldview_premises.support: San Francisco Fed 40-year cross-country study; caveat that historical tariff moves were much smaller than 2025's.

worldview_premises.premise: Central bank inflation-fighting credibility was hard won and is being squandered; once inflation is embedded (1970s) it is very hard to remove, and after the 2021-22 spike expectations are more at risk of de-anchoring.
worldview_premises.support: 1970s precedent; Fed acknowledging de-anchoring as a theoretical risk; affordability debate (prices stay high though inflation moderated).

worldview_premises.premise: Labels mislead: 'alternative' or 'private' does not mean diversifying (PE/VC are private growth; credit correlates with equities in declines), so assets should be classed as growth or diversifying with a high bar for diversifier.
worldview_premises.support: Correlation behaviour of credit in up vs down equity markets; argument by classification.

worldview_premises.premise: Investors under-allocate to true diversifiers because of capital constraints, viewing buckets in isolation, and judging strategies on a 15-year equity bull market; standalone hedge-fund optimisation drifts to convergent equity-like strategies.
worldview_premises.support: JP Morgan AM / GIC study; Markowitz logic; observation of institutional portfolios.

worldview_premises.premise: Typical institutional and wealth portfolios are concentrated in growth and stable inflation (80% growth-linked by capital, 90%+ by risk) and hold little protection against high inflation or deflationary deleveraging; tail risks are underpriced.
worldview_premises.support: Description of endowment/pension and wealth-manager allocations; 1966-82 derating of equities; IMF-economist warnings.

worldview_premises.premise: Smoother returns matter more in a regime where a large cohort is near retirement; large drawdowns near retirement are worst.

mechanism_chains.topic: Why long-term yields are rising outside the US

steps.from: AI data-centre/chip capex and rising defence spending
steps.why: Demand for savings increases relative to the old excess-savings world.

steps.from: No political appetite for austerity or fiscal restraint
steps.why: Cost-of-living pressure demands more fiscal support, and the peace dividend of the 2000s is gone.

steps.from: Savings-investment balance shifts from excess savings to scarce capital
steps.to: higher long-term yields (JGB, Bunds first; US lagging)
steps.why: The reverse of the Greenspan conundrum and 2010s negative-yield era.

mechanism_chains.evidence: Observed global yield trends; no formal test.
mechanism_chains.fails_when: US 10-year stays near 4.1%; the US is noted as the outlier so far.

mechanism_chains.topic: Debt plus equity valuation as a fragility channel

steps.to: larger fiscal deficit and a step up in debt/GDP
steps.why: Tax revenue falls and spending rises; the ratio has stepped higher in every recession.

steps.from: Equity bear market in a financialised economy
steps.to: large wealth loss and likelihood of recession
steps.why: Households hold about $40T of equities; a 2022-style bear market could erase $20T.

steps.to: higher odds of fiscal dominance and financial repression; tails of runaway inflation or deflationary deleveraging
steps.why: Policy framework and central bank independence also under threat.

mechanism_chains.evidence: Historical debt/GDP step pattern and the IMF economist estimate; qualitative.
mechanism_chains.fails_when: Not stated; presented as a risk, not a forecast.

mechanism_chains.topic: Tariff transmission to inflation and the Fed

steps.to: immediate rise in unemployment and a fall in inflation
delayed pass-through, inflation rising in the next two years
steps.why: Historical cross-country pattern; plausible delayed US impact.

steps.from: Fed cutting with inflation already above target and a split committee
steps.to: complacent market pricing and eroded inflation credibility

mechanism_chains.evidence: SF Fed 40-year study applied by analogy.
mechanism_chains.fails_when: Study moves were much smaller than 2025 tariffs, so the pattern may mis-size today's effects.

mechanism_chains.topic: Why trend following does well when inflation surprises

steps.from: Inflation expectations become less anchored or unpredictable
steps.to: sustained repricing in bonds, currencies, commodities
steps.why: Higher sensitivity after 2021-22 means shocks propagate.

steps.to: trend following profits when inflation is 1 pp above or below its two-year average
steps.why: Paper finds trend stands out among strategies in those episodes.

mechanism_chains.evidence: Paper's conditional analysis of inflation surprises.

mechanism_chains.topic: Why the adaptive portfolio compounds better than 60/40

steps.from: Adaptive strategies add risk when equities trend up and cut it when conditions change
steps.to: rolling equity beta swinging from negative to above one
steps.why: Trend acts as a midfielder, not purely defence.

steps.to: compounding from a higher base after recoveries

steps.from: Balanced risk across growth, inflation and deflation scenarios
steps.to: robustness rather than outperformance in every period
steps.why: 2015-2019 was best for 60/40; the design targets the next 10 years under uncertainty.

mechanism_chains.evidence: Backtest since 1990 versus 60/40 (hypothetical); better even in the disinflation period.
mechanism_chains.fails_when: Underperforms in strong-bond, low-inflation bull periods such as 2015-2019.

decision_process.practice: Allocate risk 40% to growth, 40% to adaptive strategies (trend, macro), 20% to diversifying assets and strategies.
decision_process.why: Growth-oriented over the long run, with diversifiers for risk-adjusted return and a high adaptive share to reflect the new macro regime.

decision_process.practice: Think in risk contribution, not capital weights; choose the best risk-adjusted blend first, then set the risk level with leverage or deleverage (futures, return stacking, portable alpha).
decision_process.why: Markowitz logic; capital constraints otherwise force equity as the only way to raise risk.

decision_process.practice: Treat adaptive strategies as the mechanism that tilts the portfolio's risk posture, not as a crisis-hedge bucket; target ~8% tracking error to 60/40 (CalPERS ~4% to 75/25).
decision_process.why: More flexibility than a total-portfolio approach anchored to a reference portfolio.

decision_process.practice: Class assets only as growth or diversifying, with a higher bar for diversifiers; private equity and venture capital count as growth.
Judge diversifying strategies on a total-portfolio view and not on the past 15-year equity bull market; show results across eras including 2015-2019.
decision_process.why: Standalone or bull-market judgement biases toward convergent equity-like strategies.

decision_process.practice: Rebalance wealth portfolios away from 50-60% equities, 20% fixed income with little gold/hedge funds toward inflation and deflation protection.
decision_process.why: Tail risks are underpriced and portfolios are unprepared.

decision_process.practice: Reclassify return-stacked products as 'unconstrained multiasset' rather than 'levered multiasset'.
decision_process.why: The leverage label can restrict platform distribution; the products integrate long/short and leverage.

speakers.evidence_style: Mix of historical episodes and narrative regime analysis, cited third-party studies (SF Fed, McKinsey, St. Louis Fed, JPM/GIC), and a hypothetical backtest since 1990 of his own paper portfolio; says he runs such a portfolio with his own money.

current_views.view: Hassett is the likely next Fed chair (Polymarket ~70%, peaked ~80%) and would likely be more dovish.
current_views.reasoning: Betting-market moves are read as informed money; Hassett is a supply-side economist aligned with the administration's productivity-boom view.

current_views.view: Markets are complacent about Fed cuts with inflation above target and tariff pass-through still to come; the Fed is split.
current_views.reasoning: SF Fed study pattern; stalled progress to 2%.

current_views.view: A yen carry unwind would be negative for trend followers who are short yen, especially crosses, with severity depending on speed and context.
current_views.reasoning: Trend followers have been positioned short yen during a persistent, prolonged weakness.

current_views.view: Global bond yields are trending higher and the US may follow; the AI/1990s equity parallel is superficial and the backdrop is riskier.
current_views.reasoning: Savings-investment shift, high debt, elevated valuations.

current_views.view: Trend following need not be permanently hurt by policy reversals; the question is unknowable but past choppy phases passed.

speakers.name: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
speakers.role: Host, Top Traders Unplugged; former CTA manager; runs trend barometer
speakers.speaker_note: Host who also states views on trend, fed independence and market structure; most data recitations (index performance, SocGen cutoffs) are factual reporting.

worldview_premises.premise: Intuition that policy-reversal chop favours short-term trading is wrong in practice: short-term trend strategies had a very bad 2025.
worldview_premises.support: SocGen short-term traders index -5.41% YTD, large for its volatility.

worldview_premises.premise: A few discrete events can determine a trend manager's year (e.g. Liberation Day), so evaluation should take a long-term view.
worldview_premises.support: Conversation with another manager whose outperformance came around Liberation Day.

worldview_premises.premise: Trend should do well when inflation is unstable even if not high.
worldview_premises.support: Intuition posed as a question; he is unsure whether research exists.

worldview_premises.premise: The biggest investor mistake is assuming present conditions persist (Marks) and financial systems always break down (White).
worldview_premises.support: Quotes of Howard Marks and Bill White.

worldview_premises.premise: The stock-bond correlation turns positive whenever rates exceed about 3-4%, across 125 years of data.
worldview_premises.support: Long historical data, recalled not shown.

worldview_premises.premise: Closeness of the likely Fed chair to the administration puts Fed independence in doubt.
worldview_premises.support: Observation that the candidate defends administration policy on TV.

worldview_premises.premise: Crabel's largest strategy now being trend, and the high SocGen AUM cutoffs, suggest long-term trend is more viable than short-term and large managers dominate indices.
worldview_premises.support: Index membership observations; flagged as his own words.

decision_process.practice: Monitor a trend barometer (39 on 1 Dec 2025: neutral-to-weak) and index performance as a pulse of the CTA industry.
decision_process.why: Gives a read on near-term trend manager performance.

speakers.evidence_style: Industry data points (indices, barometer, AUM cutoffs), anecdotes from other guests, and quoted authorities.

current_views.view: Trend followers had five or six consecutive positive months into Nov 2025 after a tough start; 2025 indices are about flat (SocGen CTA -1.6%, Trend +0.2%) versus MSCI World +20.7%.
Vanguard allowing crypto funds is positive for crypto distribution; a possible MSCI removal of Strategy could force index-tracker selling.
Trend exposure to Japan may sit more in JGBs than outright yen.
current_views.reasoning: Offered as a twist, not verified.

current_views.view: AI adoption is widespread (McKinsey: 20% in 2017 to 88%).
The 'levered multiasset' Morningstar label could restrict distribution of return-stacked products.

gaps_and_conflicts.issue: Backtest results of the adaptive portfolio are hypothetical and given only qualitatively on the show (outperformance since 1990 via smaller drawdowns); no Sharpe, costs or implementation detail stated.
The SF Fed tariff study uses much smaller historical tariff moves than the 2025 US tariffs; the claim of delayed inflation is applied by analogy and the speaker also says it is 'plausible'.
The $20T wealth-loss figure is attributed to a former IMF chief economist, not derived by the speaker.
Host's claim that trend does better when inflation is unstable is intuition; Dunne's paper provides only a 1 pp surprise test.
Inconsistency in reasoning: US yields flagged as rising pressure yet the US 10-year (4.1%) is the outlier; no mechanism given for why the US lags.
Claim that Crabel's growth in trend shows long-term strategies are more viable than short-term is the host's inference from one firm.
Prediction-market inference that Hassett's rise reflects informed money is speculation.
Trend barometer details and index AUM cutoffs are factual updates with no forecasting content.
The comparison with the 125-year stock-bond correlation threshold of 3-4% is stated from memory without a source.

forward_looking_inputs: (reader) Inputs said to lead prices: inflation surprises versus two-year average (trend payoff), Fed chair appointment and path of cuts versus inflation above target, tariff pass-through over 2 years, savings-investment balance shown in global long yields (JGB, Bund, US 10-year), debt/GDP and equity valuation (fiscal dominance risk), stock-bond correlation sign tied to rate level above 3-4%. Horizons are quarters to a decade; portfolio-level robustness is framed over 'the next 10 years'.
reader_inferences: (reader) Dunne's thesis is a chain from regime change (higher, stickier inflation) to unstable stock-bond correlation to the need for flexible risk-posture strategies; the logical weak point is that the evidence for the new regime is mostly narrative.
(reader) The 40/40/20 split by risk is a normative design rather than an optimised result; no optimisation procedure is described.
(reader) The tariff-inflation view is a delayed-effect argument that would be falsified if inflation does not rise over the following two years.

(reader) Host and guest are aligned throughout; there is no substantive disagreement, only differences of emphasis (host questions on AI adoption, fiscal dominance and inflation instability are answered by the guest, not contested).
